title: Getting around
goal: Ask for and give directions, take a rickshaw or bus, and tell someone what to do.
intro:
To give directions you need the **imperative** — and in Urdu it comes in three levels of politeness that match آپ, تم and تو. With strangers, drivers and shopkeepers, use the polite **آپ** forms (چلیے، رکیے، بتائیے), and soften them further with ذرا (zarā, 'just').

You'll also learn how to say 'to', 'from', 'up to' and 'towards' a place with postpositions.

grammar.title: The imperative: three levels
grammar.body:
Each 'you' has its own command form, built on the verb stem:

**تو** (intimate/rude): bare stem — رک! جا! بیٹھ!
**تم** (familiar): stem + **و** -o — رکو، جاؤ، بیٹھو
**آپ** (polite): stem + **یے** -iye — رکیے، جائیے، بیٹھیے

A second polite form, stem + **یں** -eṃ (رکیں، جائیں، بیٹھیں), is very common in speech and slightly softer — it also means 'let's…'.

A few verbs are irregular in the آپ form: کرنا → **کیجیے**, دینا → **دیجیے**, لینا → **لیجیے**, پینا → **پیجیے**. In the تم form: دینا → دو, لینا → لو, کرنا → کرو.

Negative commands use **نہ** na (or مت mat, more blunt): یہاں نہ رکیے 'please don't stop here'.

Soften with **ذرا** zarā 'just' or **پلیز**: ذرا رکیے 'just wait a moment, please'.

examples.en: Here's your ticket. (lit. take this ticket)

grammar.title: Going to, coming from: direction postpositions
grammar.body:
With verbs of motion, the destination usually needs **no postposition** at all: میں بازار جا رہا ہوں 'I'm going (to the) market'. (کو is possible but less common with places.)

**سے** = from: لاہور سے 'from Lahore'
**تک** = up to, as far as: اسٹیشن تک 'as far as the station'
**کی طرف** = towards: مسجد کی طرف 'towards the mosque'
**پر** = at (a stop, a corner): اگلے چوک پر 'at the next roundabout'
**میں** = in, into: ٹیکسی میں بیٹھیے 'get in the taxi'

Remember the oblique: masculine nouns in -ā become -e: اگلا → اگلے چوک پر, کونا → کونے پر.

dialogue.title: Taking a rickshaw
dialogue.setting: Lucy flags down a rickshaw in Lahore to go to the Badshahi Mosque.

lines.speaker: Lucy
lines.en: Brother, will you go to the Badshahi Mosque?

lines.speaker: Lucy
lines.native: ٹھیک ہے۔ ذرا آہستہ چلائیے، پلیز۔
lines.roman: ṭhīk hai. zarā āhista chalā’iye, plīz.
lines.en: OK. Drive a little slowly, please.

lines.speaker: Driver
lines.native: فکر نہ کریں، باجی۔ … یہ لیں، مسجد آ گئی۔
lines.roman: fikr na kareṃ, bājī. … ye leṃ, masjid ā ga’ī.
lines.en: Don't worry, sister. … Here you are, we've arrived at the mosque.

lines.speaker: Lucy
lines.native: یہاں روک دیں۔ یہ لیجیے، شکریہ!
lines.roman: yahāṃ rok deṃ. ye lījiye, shukriya!
lines.en: Stop here, please. Here you are, thanks!

culture: Directions in Pakistan are usually given by landmarks — a mosque, a petrol pump, a famous sweet shop — rather than street names. Rickshaw and taxi fares are agreed before you get in (or use a ride-hailing app). On buses and in some rickshaws there may be separate seating for women. Drivers, waiters and shopkeepers are commonly addressed as بھائی or بھائی جان, and women as باجی or آپی.
